Chapter One

A consulting detective, a doctor, and a magazine

In gaslit Victorian and Edwardian London, a “consulting detective” — Holmes's own invented job title — solves by observation and reasoning what Scotland Yard cannot, while his friend Dr John Watson narrates, grounding genius in an ordinary reader's eyes.

That is the whole engine, and it never really changes across forty years of stories. A client climbs the seventeen steps to 221B Baker Street. Holmes reads their boots, cuffs, and calluses like a newspaper. Watson — brave, loyal, and perpetually a half-step behind, exactly as the reader is — asks the questions we would ask. Then the reasoning is laid out, link by link, and what looked like magic turns out to have been attention.

Built like a subscription

Most of the canon is short stories, published monthly and self-contained in The Strand Magazine. A commuter could buy one issue, read one complete case on the train, and need nothing before or after it. Fiction built like a subscription — a familiar detective, a fresh puzzle, every month.

Seen through Watson

Holmes the character is seen almost entirely through Watson. We rarely get Holmes's thoughts directly; we get his effects — on clients, on policemen, on his friend. The genius stays mysterious because the camera is never inside his head.

The central idea

The world is legible. Mud, ash, a worn cuff, a tan line — everything is evidence, if someone has trained himself to notice. Holmes is less a magician than a demonstration that attention is a skill.

Chapter Two

The canon: four novels, fifty-six stories

Everything in this primer — the characters, methods, places, and myths — comes from those sixty tales and nothing else. That boundary is what scholars mean by “the canon.” Search any title, and open a collection to see its stories.

The whole canon is in the public domain, and every tale below carries a Read free line: external links to free editions of the full text at Standard Ebooks and Project Gutenberg. For a short story, the links open the collection that contains it.

The novels, in publication order

Novel One
1887

A Study in Scarlet

First published in Beeton's Christmas Annual. Watson, invalided home from Afghanistan, meets Holmes at St Bartholomew's Hospital, and the Lauriston Gardens murder follows. Doyle reportedly sold the full copyright for £25 — one of the great bad bargains in publishing.

Read free (external, public domain): Standard Ebooks ↗ · Project Gutenberg ↗

Novel Two
1890

The Sign of the Four

Commissioned by Lippincott's at the same famous dinner that produced Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray. It introduces Mary Morstan, Watson's future wife, and brings back Holmes's paid corps of street children, the Baker Street Irregulars, first seen in A Study in Scarlet.

Read free (external, public domain): Standard Ebooks ↗ · Project Gutenberg ↗

Novel Three
1902

The Hound of the Baskervilles

Serialized in the Strand in 1901–02. Written after Holmes's apparent death at Reichenbach, but set earlier — a ghost from the past, in every sense. Dartmoor, a spectral hound, and the most famous detective novel ever written.

Read free (external, public domain): Standard Ebooks ↗ · Project Gutenberg ↗

Novel Four
1915

The Valley of Fear

Serialized 1914–15. A two-part structure: an English country-house murder, then an American back-story echoing the real Molly Maguires case among Pennsylvania miners — with Professor Moriarty looming behind it all.

Read free (external, public domain): Standard Ebooks ↗ · Project Gutenberg ↗

No tale in the canon matches that — the dog did nothing in the night-time.

A note on the count

Count the listings in the five collections and you reach fifty-seven — but one of them, “The Adventure of the Cardboard Box,” is the same story keeping two homes: it sits in The Memoirs in early British editions and in His Last Bow in many later ones. Counted once: fifty-six stories, plus the four novels, make the sixty tales of the canon.

A life, as best it can be dated

Doyle was cheerfully inconsistent with dates. These are the traditional dates Holmesian scholars reconstruct — when events happened inside the stories, from the meeting at St Bart’s in 1881 to the last bow in 1914. Chapter Four Real world · Publishing order

Forty years in print, 1887–1927

The chronology above dates Holmes’s life inside the stories. This timeline dates the stories themselves — the real-world record of how the canon reached its readers, from a Christmas annual in 1887 to the final collection forty years later. Same tales, different order — and the difference is the story. Tap any entry to unfold it, or filter by kind.

Story-world order — Chronology

When Holmes lived it: 1881 meeting → 1891 fall at Reichenbach → 1894 return → 1914 last bow. The Hound belongs before the fall.

Real-world order — this timeline

When readers got it: Doyle published the fall in 1893, then published the Hound in 1901–02 anyway — a “new” novel with Holmes already dead, set before the fall.

Show:
Read the two timelines against each other

Doyle published the fall in 1893, yet set the Hound before it — which is how a “new” Holmes novel could appear in 1901 with Holmes already dead. Publication order is the order readers experienced the death, the long silence, and the return; story-world order is the order Holmes lived them. The primer keeps both, labelled, so the two never blur.

Every story, in publication order

The collections gathered the stories in one order; the magazines published them in another. This list follows first magazine publication, story by story — all fifty-six, numbered in the order readers first met them. Era:
Where the order surprises

Two traps for the unwary. “The Cardboard Box” (no. 14) was left out of the first British Memoirs and sits in His Last Bow in American editions — an 1893 story in a 1917 book. And The Case-Book opens with “The Illustrious Client” (no. 50 here) although five of its stories were published earlier.

Chapter Five

Arthur Conan Doyle: the doctor who became a writer

Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle was born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859, into an Irish Catholic family long on talent and short on money.

Edinburgh, 1859–1876 · A storyteller's son

His father, Charles Altamont Doyle, was a gifted artist whose career dissolved in alcoholism. His mother, Mary Foley Doyle, held the family together and filled the house with tales of chivalry. Sent at nine to Stonyhurst, a Jesuit school whose discipline he hated, he discovered he could hold other boys spellbound by inventing stories.

Medicine, 1876–1882 · The pupil of Joseph Bell

At Edinburgh he studied medicine and served as clerk to Dr Joseph Bell, who could read a patient's trade and travels from a glance. Years later he wrote to Bell that it was most certainly to him that he owed Sherlock Holmes. Between terms he shipped as surgeon on an Arctic whaler and a West African steamer.

Southsea, 1882–1891 · Writing in the waiting room

He set up practice at Southsea, married Louisa Hawkins in 1885, and wrote fiction while patients did not come. A Study in Scarlet — written in three weeks — appeared in 1887, its copyright sold for £25. The Sign of the Four followed from the 1889 Lippincott's dinner that also commissioned Wilde's Dorian Gray.

The books he prized · Historical novels and Professor Challenger

Doyle valued almost everything he wrote above Holmes. He believed his reputation would rest on his historical fiction: Micah Clarke (1889), The White Company (1891), and Sir Nigel (1906). Science fiction gave him a second famous creation in Professor Challenger of The Lost World (1912).

1891 — the year it turned

The Strand short stories made him famous within months. He abandoned medicine — first for an eye specialist's rooms in London where, by his own cheerful account, not a single patient ever walked in. It was the luckiest failure of his life.

The man who tried to outgrow his detective. Doyle valued almost everything he wrote above Holmes. Posterity disagreed — and his long argument with his own creation is the second half of his story.

1893–1903 · Killing Holmes, and bringing him back

Tired of the detective crowding out his higher work, he told his mother he was thinking of slaying Holmes — and in “The Final Problem” (1893) he did. The Strand, said to have lost 20,000 subscriptions, pressed him for a decade; in 1903, for a very large Collier's fee, “The Empty House” brought Holmes back.

The public man · Soldier, knight, and real-life detective

Too old to enlist at forty, he served as a physician at a Bloemfontein field hospital in the Boer War, wrote The Great Boer War (1900), and was knighted in 1902 — for the war work, not for Holmes. He campaigned against the Belgian atrocities in The Crime of the Congo (1909), and twice played Holmes in earnest: helping to clear George Edalji (1907) and to free Oscar Slater, whose 1927 release he worked — and paid much of the appeal costs — to win.

The last decade · Grief, spiritualism, and the fairies

Louisa died in 1906; he married Jean Leckie in 1907. The war took his son Kingsley in 1918 and his brother Innes in 1919. Doyle became spiritualism's most famous champion — The History of Spiritualism (1926), and The Coming of the Fairies (1922), defending photographs confessed as a hoax only in 1983. His friendship with Houdini broke over the belief.

Steel true, blade straight

He died at Crowborough on 7 July 1930; his last words, to Jean, are reported as “You are wonderful.” His gravestone reads: “Steel true, blade straight — Knight, Patriot, Physician and man of letters.” Fiction's most rational creator spent his final decade arguing for seances and fairies, insisting he was simply following the evidence.

Chapter Six

The players of Baker Street

The detective, the doctor who tells it, the household, the Yard, the brother — and the three opponents who were truly worth his attention. Choose a name to open the dossier.

The partnership

Holmes supplies the reasoning; Watson supplies the world — warmth, courage, common sense, and an audience. Neither works alone. The canon is, underneath every puzzle, a forty-year friendship.

Chapter Seven

The methods

Holmes sets out his “science of deduction” in an article in A Study in Scarlet — the article Watson mocks, written by the flatmate he has just met. Its rules, in Holmes's own words:

“You see, but you do not observe.”

A Scandal in Bohemia

“It is a capital mistake to theorize before one has data.”

A Scandal in Bohemia

“Data! data! data! I can't make bricks without clay.”

The Adventure of the Copper Beeches

“When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.”

The Sign of the Four

“The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes.”

The Hound of the Baskervilles

“There is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact.”

The Boscombe Valley Mystery

The monographs

Holmes writes specialist studies no one else thought to write: on distinguishing 140 forms of tobacco ash, on tracing footsteps, and on how a man's trade marks his handwriting and his hands. Expertise, for Holmes, is a filing system built in advance of the case that will need it.

An actor in Baker Street

Holmes's disguises are actor-grade — an old woman, a clergyman, a plumber — and Watson repeatedly fails to recognize his own flatmate until the reveal. The disguise is not vanity; it is how a famous face gathers evidence nobody would give to Sherlock Holmes.

The Baker Street Irregulars

His paid corps of street children, under their leader Wiggins, can go everywhere, see everything, and overhear what no adult could. Holmes pays a shilling a day and treats them as professionals — the city's smallest intelligence service.

Ahead of the science

In 1887 Holmes opens the canon by inventing a chemical test for bloodstains — years before forensic blood testing was practical. In “The Adventure of the Norwood Builder” (1903), a thumbprint nearly hangs an innocent man, and Holmes exposes it as a fake — when forensic fingerprinting was brand new.

Doyle as detective

Twice, Doyle played detective himself, campaigning to free two real prisoners: George Edalji, cleared in 1907, and Oscar Slater, released in 1927. The method — re-examine the evidence, distrust the easy story — was Holmes's, applied to real life.

Chapter Eight

“You see, but you do not observe”

Holmes's method, as a parlour exercise. Read the scene as Watson saw it — then answer as Holmes would. The clues are all in the text; nothing is hidden that Holmes would not have seen.

A client has just been shown into the sitting room at 221B. Watson, watching from his chair, notes what any of us would:

A man of about forty, neatly dressed but not expensively. There is red clay mud on his boots, still damp. His right cuff is dusted with white chalk, and the skin of his right forefinger and thumb is rough and stained yellow-brown. On his watch-chain hangs a brass key, much worn. He carries a railway timetable, folded open and soft with use, and before he sits he glances at the clock and says he must not miss the 4:15 back to his school — though he has plainly come up to London in a hurry, and on a weekday morning.

Chapter Eleven

The template detective fiction still follows

William Gillette's 1899 stage play fixed the visual image of Holmes for the world; he performed the role more than a thousand times over some thirty years, and generations pictured Holmes as Gillette played him.

Guinness World Records has credited Holmes as the most portrayed literary character in film and television, with hundreds of screen portrayals since 1900. The Baker Street Irregulars, founded in New York in 1934 by Christopher Morley, seeded a worldwide society of “Sherlockians” who play the Great Game — treating Holmes and Watson as real men, and Doyle as merely Watson's literary agent.

Letters addressed to Sherlock Holmes have been arriving at 221B Baker Street for a century, and a museum at 221B now recreates the sitting room for visitors — a fictional address, staffed like a real one, because readers insisted.

The deeper legacy

The canon set the template — the eccentric genius, the loyal narrator-friend, the locked room, the clue the reader saw too — that nearly all detective fiction still follows. Every consulting detective since, on page or screen, works in a room Holmes furnished.

Sources, credits, and uncertainties

All texts referenced are Arthur Conan Doyle's public-domain canon: the four novels (1887–1915) and the five short-story collections (1892–1927). In-universe dates are traditional reconstructions — Doyle contradicted himself freely (Watson's war wound famously migrates between shoulder and leg), and no chronology can be more exact than its author allowed. Claims about records and performance counts are stated with the hedges used in the primer text.

All six illustrations are original artworks created for the Sherlock Holmes Primer, in homage to Sidney Paget's public-domain Strand illustration style. No film or television imagery, no actor likenesses, and no material from any modern adaptation has been used. This interactive edition presents the primer's contents in browsable form.

“The game is afoot.” — Sixty tales: four novels and fifty-six short stories. Everything else, including this page, is commentary.
